This site pairs two ways of studying Scripture: browse the whole Bible chronologically to see what era, king, or prophet surrounded any book, or open one of the six books written out in full to read it verse by verse alongside its cross-references and how four Christian traditions — Wesleyan, Reformed, Catholic, and Anabaptist — have read each passage.

Every Book, By Genre

Or jump straight to a book, grouped the way a study Bible's own contents page would — the Law, History, Wisdom, the Prophets, the Gospels, and the Epistles. Books in full (with cross-references and tradition notes) are marked with a dot; the rest open to their place on the timeline.

Every book of the Bible, arranged by the era of history it belongs to — Old Testament flowing left to right, then New Testament continuing after the roughly four centuries of prophetic silence between the Testaments. Click any book to read it; use the filters to see which king, prophet, or figure was center stage at a given point in the story.

Dates are approximate and follow one widely used scholarly framework — several, especially the earliest Old Testament books and a handful of contested New Testament epistles, are genuinely disputed among scholars. Books marked with a dashed edge below have the most debated dating.

How to read this: the tradition notes are short, plain-language sketches meant for comparison while studying — not official denominational statements. They're a starting point for asking "why might a Methodist, a Reformed believer, a Catholic, or an Anabaptist weigh this verse differently," not the last word on any of them. Commentary links point to outside sites (GotQuestions, Enduring Word, Desiring God, Blue Letter Bible) so you can dig deeper — their content isn't reviewed or endorsed here.

Words in red are Jesus's own words, following the traditional "red-letter" Bible convention, marked verse by verse throughout — narration, and the words of other speakers (John the Baptist, the devil, angels, disciples), stay in the ordinary text color.
